newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: U.S. aid freeze halts programmes in Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. aid freeze halts programmes in Cambodia.

text.p: Non-profit agencies reliant on U.S. funding have begun to pack their bags and close some programmes in Cambodia as a freeze on aid from Washington hit home, aid workers said on Sunday.
The United States announced on Thursday it was suspending its Cambodia aid programme for 30 days after powerful Second Prime Minister Hun Sen took full power of the country by force.
The aid suspension, which could be extended or lifted after the 30-day freeze, will affect programmes ranging from education to health to road-building, aid workers said.

At the offices of the U.S. government's largest single aid project in Cambodia, the $30-million Cambodia Assistance to Primary Education Programme (CAPE), expatriate workers were preparing to say goodbye, if only temporarily.

"We're suspending our programme. People are gathering their things and figuring out where to go and what to do for the next 30 days. They're disappointed, because our work was going well," said CAPE Chief of Party Robert Ressegnie.
Hun Sen's forces ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh in two days of fierce fighting in the Cambodian capital last weekend, provoking international concern.
The German government has also suspended aid, and France, while it has not suspended its current programme, has not yet pledged expected funds to Cambodia for the next year.
Australia is also reconsidering its aid programme.

So far the U.S. government's suspension of its $35 million aid programme is the biggest blow to Cambodia's $500 million international assistance package, which accounts for half of the national budget.

U.S.-funded staff are required to leave the country within 10 days of the suspension order after securing their offices and locking up their assets, including trucks and other equipment, U.S. embassy staff said.

Hundreds of aid workers have already left the country, some out of continued concern over their safety. Several told Reuters their staff had been held up by police or soldiers during the recent violence in the capital and they were worried about general lawlessness.

Aid workers said the aid freeze was a tough blow in a country where the per capita annual income is less than $300, most people are poor farmers and young children die unnecessarily of diarrhoea and other preventable diseases.

"I don't think the Cambodian government cares if the non-profit sector is hurt or if social services are hit. They haven't been providing those services anyway," said one U.S. aid worker. "It's the Cambodian people who will be affected."
A Cambodian analyst said local organisations heavily dependent on foreign funding were vulnerable.
"A number of local organisations will go down the drain. This will kill them," he said.

CAPE, which is 100-percent funded by the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), has to send all expatriate staff out of the country, Ressegnie said, effectively halting all teacher training.
Other aid agencies that receive only partial U.S. funding are struggling to find a way to stay open for business in what is one of the world's poorest countries, workers said.

Mark Pierce, country representative of Catholic Relief Services, said he has had to send out three international staff for safety reasons but wanted to keep his programmes afloat through extra funds from his own office.
That includes U.S.-funded village banks that provide 3,000 poor women with small loans.
"The banks are still meeting," he said. "As long as it remains relatively quiet, we'll stay."
